explanation:
[FEATURE: hr]
[EFFECT] Hour of day has a strongly non-monotonic, two-peak effect. Demand is heavily suppressed in the early-morning hours (0–5), reaching its lowest point around 4 a.m. (contribution near –2.8). It then rises sharply to a morning peak at 8 a.m. (~+1.1), dips slightly mid-morning, and climbs again to the highest positive contributions at 5–6 p.m. (hours 17–18, ~+1.2 to +1.3), before declining again after 10 p.m. and turning slightly negative at midnight.
[IMPORTANCE] This is by far the strongest feature (importance 0.889); its effect dwarfs every other feature in the model.

[FEATURE: temp]
[EFFECT] Temperature has a non-monotonic effect: very cold conditions (normalised temp near 0, i.e. close to 0 °C) strongly suppress demand (contribution around –1.5), and demand climbs steadily as temperature rises, peaking around a normalised value of 0.75 (roughly 31 °C, contribution ~+0.3). At the highest temperatures (near 41 °C) the contribution turns slightly negative again, suggesting extreme heat marginally reduces rentals.
[IMPORTANCE] This is the second most important feature (importance 0.253), with a wide vertical range of roughly 1.8 log units.

[FEATURE: yr]
[EFFECT] Year acts as a single step change: hours in 2011 (yr = 0) carry a contribution of about –0.23, while hours in 2012 (yr = 1) carry a contribution of about +0.20, reflecting roughly 40% higher baseline demand in the second year of operation.
[IMPORTANCE] Third in importance (0.217); though simple in shape, the shift between years is sizeable and affects every prediction.

[FEATURE: mnth]
[EFFECT] Month has a non-monotonic effect. Winter months are negative drivers: January (~–0.25) and February (~–0.20) most strongly suppress demand. Contributions rise through spring, are near zero in summer (July–August), and peak in autumn — especially October (~+0.35 to +0.37) — before easing in November and December.
[IMPORTANCE] Fourth in importance (0.086); a moderate influence, spanning roughly 0.6 log units.

[FEATURE: hum]
[EFFECT] Humidity has a non-monotonic shape with a sharp early jump. At extremely low humidity (below ~5%) demand is strongly suppressed (~–1.0). Contribution jumps quickly to a slight positive plateau (~+0.10) at moderate humidity and stays roughly flat up to about 60%, then gradually declines, reaching about –0.3 at 100% humidity.
[IMPORTANCE] Fifth in importance (0.083), close to month; the extreme low-humidity penalty is notable but affects relatively few hours.

[FEATURE: weathersit]
[EFFECT] Weather acts as a step function across four categories. Clear skies (category 1) give a small positive boost (~+0.045); mist/cloud (2) is nearly neutral (~0); light rain or snow (3) substantially suppresses demand (~–0.35); and heavy rain (4) also suppresses demand (~–0.25) — slightly less than category 3 in this model.
[IMPORTANCE] Sixth in importance (0.061); meaningful but smaller in magnitude than temperature or year.

[FEATURE: weekday]
[EFFECT] Weekday has a modest, roughly increasing effect from Sunday to Friday. Sunday (0) carries the most negative contribution (~–0.065), Monday is slightly negative, midweek days are near zero, and Friday (5) has the highest positive contribution (~+0.040), with Saturday slightly lower. The total range is only about 0.1 log units.
[IMPORTANCE] Seventh in importance (0.024); a real but small effect — day of week matters far less than time of day or temperature.

[FEATURE: windspeed]
[EFFECT] Wind speed has a mostly flat contribution at low speeds (below roughly 0.2 normalised, i.e. below ~13 km/h) and then monotonically decreases as wind increases, reaching around –0.35 at the highest observed speeds (~55 km/h). The decline becomes steeper above a normalised value of about 0.3.
[IMPORTANCE] Eighth in importance (0.014); a minor feature whose penalty only becomes noticeable at quite high wind speeds.

[FEATURE: holiday]
[EFFECT] Holiday is a binary step: non-holiday hours have a near-zero contribution (~+0.01), while holiday hours produce a small negative contribution (~–0.145), indicating slightly lower predicted demand on public holidays.
[IMPORTANCE] Lowest importance of all features (0.008); the effect is negligible in practical terms.

[RECOMMENDATION] Hour of day and temperature are by far the two strongest drivers of predicted demand, so operational planning — such as bike redistribution and staffing — should be tightly organised around the two daily rush-hour peaks (around 8 a.m. and 5–6 p.m.) and scaled up noticeably in mild to warm weather while scaling back during cold spells or the early hours of the morning.
